summary: This work compares how bit-flip ($X$) and phase-flip ($Z$) Pauli noise asymmetrically affect QAOA performance on a flight-gate assignment problem, finding that bit-flip errors cause larger degradation in the optimized cost across layer-level and gate-level noise models. The authors exploit this asymmetry to propose using asymmetric quantum error-correction codes, demonstrating that a $(5,3)$ quantum parity code achieves performance comparable to a symmetric $(5,5)$ code while using 10 fewer physical qubits.
motivation: Understanding how different error types affect variational quantum algorithms is critical for the early fault-tolerant era, where error-correction resources are limited. QAOA alternates between $Z$-structured cost evolutions and $X$-structured mixer evolutions, so $X$ and $Z$ errors need not impact the algorithm equally.
method: Simulations on a 6-qubit flight-gate assignment instance mapped to an Ising Hamiltonian compare noisy QAOA performance under independent bit-flip and phase-flip channels at both layer-level (noise after each QAOA layer) and gate-level (noise after each elementary gate) using two circuit decompositions: CNOT-based and native $R_{ZZ}$ gates. Logical error rates from quantum parity codes are then applied to the simulation data to assess asymmetric error correction.
result: Bit-flip noise consistently produces larger degradation in residual cost $\Delta = C_{\mathrm{best}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{min}}$ than phase-flip noise, with asymmetry most pronounced in native-$R_{ZZ}$ and layer-level models. An asymmetric $(5,3)$ quantum parity code achieves nearly identical performance improvement as a symmetric $(5,5)$ code, using 15 instead of 25 physical qubits per logical qubit.
